feed.title: Combined summary - post-quantum: solution ideas to "tripwire"game-theory issues + a certificate-based rescue protocol

entry.title: Combined summary - post-quantum: solution ideas to "tripwire"game-theory issues + a certificate-based rescue protocol
entry.summary: The exploration of advanced blockchain security solutions in anticipation of quantum computing threats involves complex and innovative strategies that aim to mitigate potential risks. One such proposal integrates a New UTXO Model Space (NUMS) point spend as an intrinsic proof of work within the coinbase output, which could significantly increase the chain work of a block by a factor comparable to 20 times the last period's difficulty. This adjustment would alter the consensus mechanism to rely less on hash power majority, potentially reducing the influence of malicious actors within the network. Another technique employs group signatures from post-quantum upgraded coins to assign additional "weight" to blocks. These blocks incorporate a Merkle tree of signatures, enhancing the proof of order through a threshold system designed to activate a "tripwire." Despite its resistance to quantum decryption, this method does pose risks associated with social manipulation, where consensus could be unfairly swayed by a majority. To address vulnerabilities specifically for EC coin owners against cryptographic quantum computer (CRQC) threats, leveraging the Bitcoin blockchain as a secure timestamping service for certificates of discreet log knowledge has been proposed. These certificates provide a historical proof of ownership essential when conventional cryptographic methods fail under quantum capabilities. Furthermore, the concept of incorporating tripwire proofs into mining offers a strategic advantage by necessitating greater hash power from potential attackers to achieve censorship, thus making attacks like the "51% attack" more challenging. The implementation of such measures, however, would require a hard fork, prompting concerns about nodes that do not upgrade and the implications of pre-scheduled or emergency hard forks. Additional considerations include the risk of premature activation by corporate entities and strategies to prevent miner collusion, possibly through a user-activated soft fork (UASF) approach that mandates active nodes to disregard any blockchain version omitting the tripwire proof. These discussions highlight the necessity of robust, quantum-resistant mechanisms to protect blockchain technology from evolving technological threats and underscore the complexity of deploying these solutions without compromising the decentralized nature and security of existing blockchain frameworks. Each approach presents unique challenges and benefits, reflecting the ongoing debate and development within the cryptocurrency community regarding the best paths forward in the face of quantum advancements.
